wording: Part A: the rock record indicates a microbial biosphere by at least 3.4 billion years ago; earlier claims are disputed because abiotic processes and contamination can mimic biosignatures.
Part A: an estimate from higher-taxonomy patterns predicts ~8.7 million (± 1.3 million SE) eukaryotic species, about 86% still undescribed.
Part A: IPBES estimates around 1 million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades, absent action.

Part A (interdependence): nearly all non-equilibrium electron transfers on Earth are driven by microbial nanomachines whose conserved core genes co-evolved with biogeochemical cycles and spread mainly by horizontal gene transfer.

Part A (humans within Earth systems): the planetary-boundaries framework names climate change and biosphere integrity as two core boundaries, each able on its own to drive the Earth system into a new state if substantially transgressed.
Part A: Daisyworld shows that a coupled biota–temperature model with a peaked growth curve stabilises temperature; it was offered as a parable, not a model of Earth.
In SIM-R6-C0, re-implemented Daisyworld kept temperature within 22.5 ± 10 °C over luminosity 0.72–1.54 (width 0.82) vs 0.83–1.07 (0.24) without life, with hysteresis between up and down sweeps.
counterevidence_limits: Seed-area floor and integration scheme are our assumptions.

wording: Part A: Kirchner argues the best available data suggest biologically mediated feedbacks will on net amplify, not reduce, Earth's sensitivity to anthropogenic climate change, contrary to strong homeostatic Gaia.
counterevidence_limits: Gaia proponents dispute the framing (not read this pass).

wording: Part A (philosophy): Leopold's land ethic ('land is a community'; right is what preserves the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community) and deep ecology extend moral concern to the living whole.
Part A: calling life the 'soul of the Earth' is a metaphor; no evidence in this pass shows Earth to be conscious or ensouled.
Part B: the core is a solid inner core within a fluid, convecting outer core; the inner core grows ~1 mm/yr as outer-core material freezes onto it, helping drive outer-core convection.
Part B: the outer-core radius is ~3480 km and inner-core radius ~1220 km; Lehmann inferred the inner core in 1936 from earthquake waves.

Part B (heat transfer): Earth acts as a heat engine driven by radiogenic decay and slow cooling; the geodynamo runs on heat from cooling and inner-core freezing and on chemical convection, with core–mantle-boundary heat flux measuring its power supply.
Part B: first-principles calculations gave core thermal and electrical conductivities 2–3 times higher than earlier estimates, with large consequences for core thermal history.
counterevidence_limits: Single computational study; later work (not read) debates these values.

wording: Part B (planetary dynamics): most plate movement occurs along narrow plate-boundary zones; four boundary types are recognised.
Part B: mantle convection is the commonly assumed driver of plate motion, but the driving mechanism remains among the 'unanswered questions'.

Part B (magnetic field): IGRF-14 dipole moment fell from 8.32×10²² (1900) to 7.69×10²² A·m² (2025), −7.6%; free ohmic decay time is ~2.4–7.3×10⁴ yr for σ = 0.5–1.5×10⁶ S/m (assumed), far shorter than the paleomagnetic record — consistent with continual regeneration.
counterevidence_limits: Decay estimate ignores inner-core and mode structure.

wording: Part B: zircon paleointensities have been read as a geodynamo by 4.2 Ga, but a later combined study found most Jack Hills zircons poor recorders, so a geodynamo before 3.5 Ga 'remains unknown'.

Part B (symbol): traditions locate vitality or mind at the heart (Stoic hêgemonikon at the heart; Chinese xin 'heart-mind'); the core is physically central to heat flow and the geodynamo, but calling it Earth's 'heart' is metaphor — no evidence of consciousness or a literal soul.
